correctness.rationale: β(p^e)=(p^(e+1)+(-1)^e)/(p+1) gives β(u)<=u, and β(m) odd iff every odd prime exponent in odd m is even. The equation forces n even; if n=2^a m with nonsquare odd m, u=β(n) even. The proof exhausts all a: for odd a use R(a)<2/3,R(t)<=3/4 giving β(u)/n<1/2; a=2 gives 3|u and β(u)/n<=(3/4)(3/4)(7/9)=7/16<1/2; even a>=4 and t=v2(u)!=2 gives <=(11/16)^2=121/256<1/2; if t=2, β(u)=3β(v) implies 3|m, so bound <=(11/16)(7/9)(3/4)=77/192<1/2. Contradiction in each branch proves odd m square. Classify parity of a into even square or twice square, disjoint by 2-adic valuation; count candidate shapes exactly. Independent multiplicative finite check through 250000 found solutions 2,4,8,128,32768, supportive only.

value.rationale: The iterated β-superimperfect classification remains open; proving that every candidate has a square odd part reduces possible prime exponent patterns and gives O(sqrt X) global sparsity of the solution set. This is a natural all-integer obstruction rather than a low-range numerological census or complete-classification claim.

final_claim: Any positive integer n satisfying 2β(β(n))=n for multiplicative alternating divisor sum β is an even perfect square or twice a perfect square; the number ≤X is at most floor(sqrt(X)/2)+floor(sqrt(X/2))=O(sqrt X).
limitations: The finite search does not establish an all-integer solution census; theorem is only a necessary condition and upper bound.
